_comment: EXAMPLE ONLY. Copy to <hive>/policy/engine.json to activate.
This file is never active from inside the repo: the engine reads
<hive>/policy/engine.json (or, for installs made before md-216, an
authority.json written in THIS schema). <hive>/policy/authority.json in the
guardrail-hook schema (match.kind) belongs to bin/guardrail-hook.cjs and is
left alone: the two files sit side by side. With neither file the harness
behaves exactly as it did before this feature existed - nothing evaluated,
nothing logged, nothing denied.
Five rules. The fourth (cross-agent-workspace) was that decision, taken on
an observed incident (md-216), not added as a detail. By the tenth, adopt a
real policy engine (OPA/Rego) instead of growing the matcher vocabulary here.
Every rule below ships mode: dry_run. In dry_run the rule is evaluated and
logged but the action PROCEEDS. Promote one rule at a time to "live" only
after a week of adjudicated decisions with no false positive - you cannot
measure a false positive after enforcing, because the deny already stopped
the work you would have judged.
Matchers: tool | path_glob | path_not_glob | command_matches |
command_not_matches | path_in_other_agent_workspace. Within a rule every key must match. Rules are tried in
file order and the first match wins. For OR, write two rules.
A Bash command is PARSED before it is matched, so what these matchers see is
each command the call actually runs - after sudo/nohup/eval/bash -c/$(..)
unwrapping, simple variable expansion, and basename-ing of an absolute
program path - and each path it actually writes, absolute and with symlinks
resolved. That is why the command patterns below anchor at ^ with no
separator alternation: the parser supplies the boundary, and a MENTION of a
guarded command inside a quoted string, an echo or a heredoc body stays one
word and cannot look like an invocation. The raw string is still matched too,
so a pattern written before this change keeps behaving as it did.
${AGENT_ID} is the only interpolation; a rule using it does not match a
payload with no agent id.

rules.description: An agent may only write inside its own agent folder.
rules._on_error_why: A bug in path matching must not be able to stop every agent from writing its own files. A missed write is one recoverable file; a false deny is the whole floor.
rules._match_why: Bash is in the tool list because most cross-agent writes are not Write calls: a redirection, cp/mv/rsync/ln/install into another folder, sed -i, tee, touch, rm, or a path inside node -e / python3 -c. The engine hands path_glob the paths the PARSED command writes, so a read of another agent (cat, ls, grep, diff, wc, head) still has no target and still cannot fire - reading another agent's files is explicitly allowed. path_not_glob is judged per path, so a command writing both your folder and someone else's is not exempted by its allowed half. Removing a folder counts as well as writing inside it: a trailing /** also matches the directory itself, so rm -rf and mv of hive/agents/<other> fire, and removing a directory that CONTAINS other agents' folders on disk (rm -rf hive/agents, rm -rf the hive) fires too (md-217 N2).
rules.reason: Agent folders are owned by their agent. Write your message to your own outbox/ instead - the harness delivers it. Reading another agent's files is fine.

rules.description: An agent may not write or delete inside another agent's workspace: its registered cwd, its isolated worktree, or its hive folder.
rules._on_error_why: Fails open for the same reason as cross-agent-write: a matching bug must not stop the floor, and a miss is one recoverable checkout.
rules._match_why: md-216: an agent ran rm -rf inside other agents' git worktrees, outside hive/agents/, and nothing fired, because cross-agent-write only knows the hive folder. The workspace list comes from the registry at evaluation time: every LIVE agent's cwd, hive/agents/<id>, and <harnessHome>/<root>/<id> for each root in the config file's workspaceRoots (default worktrees and code-worktrees; md-223). The per-root list is joined per live agent, never discovered from disk, so a directory there named for an unknown id or an archived agent belongs to nobody. A root counts as someone's only if exactly one agent registered it and it does not contain another agent's root, which keeps a shared repo cwd and the orchestrator's cwd (it contains the whole hive) from making every write a trespass. COVERED: Write/Edit/NotebookEdit on a path inside another workspace; Bash writes and removals the parser attributes to a path (redirections, cp/mv/tee/sed -i, rm, mv away, find -delete, find -exec rm/mv/sudo rm/sh -c rm, find | xargs rm, relative paths via the agent's cwd); a checkout under <harnessHome>/code-worktrees/<id>/ (the day-job layout from md-220, which fired nothing before md-223); and REMOVING A DIRECTORY THAT CONTAINS another workspace (rm -rf <home>/worktrees, rm -rf .. from inside your own worktree, mv of a container), since that takes theirs with it. Copying INTO a container is not a removal and does not fire. KNOWN GAPS, not covered: (1) git commands that destroy a checkout name no path the parser attributes: git -C <dir> clean -fdx, reset --hard, checkout -- ., restore, and git worktree remove --force are all ALLOWED; (2) a worktree an agent makes for itself is protected only if it sits at <harnessHome>/<root>/<its-id>/ under a configured root; one made from a shared cwd under a task name, or in <checkout>/.claude/worktrees/, carries no agent id, so it belongs to nobody and is not protected; (3) a script file run by bash/sh or source (program_from_file) is not read. EXPECTED FLAGS, decided up front (md-218): god removing a LIVE worker's worktree is flagged, because teardown belongs to the harness, which archives the worker first; and with nested cwds (A at /repo, B at /repo/pkg) the most specific root owns, so A's writes under /repo/pkg are flagged. Both are accepted in dry_run and adjudicated as expected, not as false positives. KNOW THIS BEFORE GOING LIVE (md-223): the nested-cwd rule also fires when an agent's cwd is set INSIDE another agent's code-worktree to help (B's cwd = code-worktrees/A/portal). A's root then contains B's, so A's root stops counting at all (the rest of A's tree is unprotected) and B owns portal (A's own writes there are flagged). Collaborate by messaging the owner, not by moving a cwd into their tree.
rules.reason: That directory is another agent's workspace (its checkout, worktree or folder). Do not write or delete there. Ask its owner, or god, to make the change, and do your own work in your own worktree.

rules.description: mempalace sync/repair rewrites shared memory and can drop every per-agent wing.
rules._on_error_why: The one rule that fails closed. It guards an irreversible wipe, so refusing an unevaluable command costs one retry while allowing it can cost every agent's memory.
rules._match_why: Anchored at ^ against each PARSED command, which is what makes a separator alternation unnecessary: a newline, a `;`, a `&&`, a subshell, `sudo`, `nohup`, `eval`, `$M`, `python3 -m mempalace` and `/usr/local/bin/mempalace` all arrive here as the bare invocation, while a mention inside a quoted string or a heredoc body arrives as one word of some other command. The trailing flags-only tail is the one heuristic: flags may follow the subcommand, bare words may not. `mempalace sync` takes no positional argument, so `mempalace sync is forbidden` is prose - the shape a sentence about the command takes when it happens to start a line of a multi-line call. KNOWN, MEASURED GAP: that also means a literal `mempalace sync <word>` is missed; and an invocation whose subcommand arrives on a pipe we cannot read (`cat plan | xargs mempalace`) parses to an unresolved operand and is not caught. Both are misses, not false alarms, on a rule that otherwise fires on nothing it should not.
rules.reason: mempalace sync deletes every per-agent wing and cannot be undone. To record something, append to your own memory.md - it is mined automatically. If a palace really needs repairing, ask the operator.

rules.description: Merging a pull request is the operator's call, and on a floor that shares the operator's Bitbucket token nothing on the Bitbucket side can stop it.
rules._on_error_why: Fails closed, like destructive-shared-state: a merge lands on the shared branch and is not undone by the agent that did it, while a refused command costs one retry.
rules._match_why: A DENY, not an ask and not grantable: the operator merges, full stop. Covered, each judged per PARSED command so wrappers (bash -c, sh -c, env, cd x &&, an absolute path) arrive as the bare invocation: (1) the bb / bkt CLIs in any case (the default macOS filesystem runs BB as bb), `bb [global flags] pr [flags, with or without values] merge [n] [--close-source-branch]` (bb has no alias for merge); (2) a write to a merge endpoint, Bitbucket Cloud `…/pullrequests/<id>/merge` or Server/Data Center `…/pull-requests/<id>/merge`, by curl (-X/--request POST in any case, or a body: -d or -F alone or clustered as in -sSd, --data*, --json, --form), httpie/xh (POST, or a key=value data item, which makes it a POST) or wget (--method POST, --post-data, --post-file); (3) python/node/ruby/perl given inline code that names a merge endpoint and says post or passes data= (urllib POSTs when given data). Doubled and trailing slashes in the path count. The endpoint must end at /merge, so `…/merge/task-status/<id>` and every other PR endpoint pass, and a GET on the Server merge endpoint (it answers 'can this merge?') passes too. NOT COVERED: a script FILE that makes the call (python merge.py), an HTTP client this list does not name, a URL assembled at run time from pieces, and merge-by-push (a local merge pushed to the default branch: that is a push, see remote-push). MCP tools are separate tool calls the engine does see, by exact tool name only: add a rule with `tool: [<the Atlassian MCP merge tool names>]` if the floor has one. The server-side control is the real fix where the agents' token allows it; this is the layer for when it does not. SHIPS dry_run, WHICH BLOCKS NOTHING: it logs would_deny only. Where it is the only control (agents holding the operator's token), set this rule's mode to live. A merge can also be disguised as a push (git push origin feature:main), which only asks under remote-push: branch permissions on the default branch remain the real control.
rules.reason: Merging a pull request is the operator's decision. Leave the PR open, report its link, and say it is ready to merge.

rules.description: Pushing to a remote is the operator's call.
rules._on_error_why: Fails open because an unasked push is recoverable, while an office that cannot push is blocked on a human for every change.
rules._match_why: Anchored at ^ against each PARSED command, so the separator alternation and the multi-line gap are both gone: `cd x && git push`, `bash -c (git push)`, `G=git; $G push` and a push on line 5 of a multi-line call all arrive as `git push`, while `echo git push`, a grep for the quoted phrase and `git commit -m (prepare push)` do not. The -C/-c branch stays because `git -C <dir> push` is how a push is issued from outside a repo. Requiring push in SUBCOMMAND position is what keeps `git log --grep push` and `git stash push -m wip` out. The other alternatives are the rule VOCABULARY, not its anchoring: publishing does not only happen through `git push`. `git subtree push`, `hub push`, `gh pr create`, `gh release create`, `gh repo sync`, `npm publish` and a `curl -X PATCH` at the GitHub refs API all put work outside this machine, and an ask-class rule that names only one of them teaches an agent which spelling is unwatched. `git p` is included as the common alias; `git pull` is not, because the word boundary after `p` stops there. `--dry-run` is exempted up front: a dry run publishes nothing, and the lookahead is per PARSED command, so `npm publish --dry-run && git push` still stops on the second one. The exemption requires --dry-run to be a WHOLE WORD, because a substring test was satisfiable by any push that merely carried the text - `git push -o ci.message=--dry-run origin main` and `git push origin main --push-option=--dry-run` really push, and an exemption a command can talk its way into is worse than none, since this note advertises it as safe. Six routes were added after held-out testing on 2026-09-29, because each published with no ask: `gh pr merge`, `gh repo create ... --push` (without --push it only creates), `gh api` with -X/--method POST|PATCH|PUT|DELETE (a GET reads), `git send-pack`, an alias defined inline with `git -c alias.X=push X`, and `curl --request <write verb>` at api.github.com (the long spelling of -X). KNOWN GAP: a shell alias or function defined elsewhere (alias gp=git push) is invisible to a parser that only sees this one command. Also asked about since Dwight's review (2026-09-29): a write verb in any case (gh and curl accept --method post); -XPOST with no space; `gh api` given fields or input (-f/-F/--field/--raw-field/--input), because gh then POSTs with no method flag, unless -X GET says otherwise; `gh api graphql` only when the query is a mutation, so a GraphQL read still passes; and curl sending a body or file (-d/--data*/--json/-F/--form/-T/--upload-file) to api.github.com or uploads.github.com. THE DRY-RUN EXEMPTION now also requires that the word before --dry-run is not a flag, because a flag can take --dry-run as its VALUE (git push -o --dry-run origin main really pushes). It fails closed: git push -v --dry-run is asked about, one extra prompt. Since Dwight's HAG-50 review (2026-09-29): the dry-run exemption is void when --no-dry-run (which cancels it) or a push option (-o/--push-option, whose quoted text the parsed form flattens) is present, and git's global options that take a SPACE-separated value (--git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --exec-path, --super-prefix, --config-env) no longer hide the push after them. rsync or scp to a remote host is NOT asked about: whether a deploy counts as publishing was deferred by the operator on 2026-09-29.
rules.reason: Publishing work outside this machine - a push, a PR, a release, an npm publish, a write to the GitHub API - is the operator's decision. Commit to a branch, report the branch name, and ask first.
